title: A chariot of parts
hook: the nun Vajira: as "chariot" names its parts together, "being" names the heaps (SN 5.10)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the nun Soma in the Blind Men's Grove, and your line, what does it matter. Today the last nun of that chapter takes Mara's question apart, and a week closes.

Mara has tried fear and he's tried insults. With the nun Vajira, sitting alone under a tree, he tries philosophy. Who made this being? Where is its maker? Where does a being come from, and where does it go when it ends? Big questions, the kind that keep a person up at two in the morning. They sound deep, and they rest on a quiet assumption. Vajira hears it. Her answer is a simile that turns up again in later Buddhist books.
screen: `MARA TRIES PHILOSOPHY.` → `WHO MADE THIS BEING?` → `A QUIET ASSUMPTION.`

segments.voice: Vajira's verse in SN 5.10 starts with a question back. Why do you take it for granted there's a being, Mara? Is that your view? Then, paraphrased: this is just a heap of formations; no being is found in it. Just as, when the parts are put together, we say the word chariot, so when the heaps are present, we speak of a being. Lay a chariot's parts out on the ground: wheels, axle, frame, seat, yoke. Which one is the chariot? Not the wheel, not the axle, not the seat. Put them together and you say chariot, and you can ride in it. But there's no extra piece called chariot hiding among the parts. A being, Vajira says, is like that: a useful name for the heaps, body, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness, working together. Then she closes: it's only suffering that comes to be, stands and passes away. Nothing but suffering arises, nothing but suffering ends. Mara's question, who made this being, falls apart, because it assumed a solid someone to be made. And the refrain: Mara, realizing the nun Vajira knows me, disappears. Later, in the Questions of King Milinda, the monk Nagasena uses the chariot to answer a Greek king, and quotes Vajira's verse. Look back at this week: forest monks who don't mourn the past, the tangle, mountains closing in, a daughter who may be better, Mara seen again by Soma, and now Vajira, taking his question apart.
screen: `WHY DO YOU ASSUME A BEING?` · `WHEELS, AXLE, SEAT: WHICH IS THE CHARIOT?` · `A BEING: A NAME FOR THE HEAPS` · `NAGASENA AND THE GREEK KING` · then, large: `A CHARIOT OF PARTS.`

segments.voice: Take one word you use about yourself, like tired, and gently take it apart: a heaviness behind the eyes, a slump in the shoulders, a thought that says I can't, a wish to lie down. Notice each part on its own; none of them alone is tired, yet together the word is useful. Then let the parts be, and rest with the breath.

Ratha. The Pali and Sanskrit word for chariot, the image in the nun Vajira's answer to Mara in SN 5.10: as chariot names the parts together, a being is a name for the heaps, with no extra someone inside. Today's word.
Your line: only suffering comes to be. No extra someone hides among the parts. A week closes here.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers in several traditions use the chariot simile, from Vajira's verse and the Questions of King Milinda, to explain not-self.

trapdoor: what you thought: a chariot of parts is a riddle about machines.
what it means: in SN 5.10, the nun Vajira's answer to Mara: being is a convenient name for the five heaps, as chariot is for its parts.
what a scholar hears: the Milindapañha's chariot dialogue between Nagasena and King Milinda, whom some historians identify with the Indo-Greek king Menander, builds on the same simile.
recall: an axe, the image for harmful speech

chat.says: Why did the nun Vajira compare a person to a chariot?
options: No single part is the chariot; 'being' names the heaps working together.
Because life moves fast, and you have to learn to steer it well.
Because Mara came riding up in one, and she turned it against him.
chat.meaning: In SN 5.10 Vajira says 'chariot' names its parts together; in the same way 'a being' names the heaps, with no extra someone inside.

formations.meaning: habits and intentions, one of the five heaps

notes: SN 5.10 paraphrased. Confirm Mara's questions (by whom was this being created, where is its maker, where does it arise and cease), Vajira's reply (why assume 'a being'; a heap of sheer formations, no being found; as 'chariot' with an assemblage of parts, so 'a being' when the aggregates exist; only suffering arises, stands and falls away).
Confirm that SN 5.10 is the last sutta of the Bhikkhuni Samyutta (the review calls Vajira the last nun of the chapter).
Confirm that Nagasena in the Milindapañha quotes Vajira's verse (Rhys Davids 1890 translation attributes it to 'our Sister Vagira'); the script says only 'quotes this kind of verse'.
Menander identification is standard but scholarly; kept in the trapdoor only.
